Meta creative review · revised 26 October 2026

Two different problems wearing the same rejection label

Meta gives all fourteen ads one reason: Online Gambling and Games. But the account contains a natural control group — sixty-three ads, one shared primary text, and five creatives that are rejected and running at the same time. Testing against it splits the fourteen into two groups: ten where a single headline word decides the outcome, and four where the creative is irrelevant and the App Store listing is the only thing that differs.

Group A — the headline is the variable

Ten ads, five images, rejected on both iOS and Android. Each belongs to a concept whose sibling variant is approved and running. Within a concept the badges, sublines, cash figures and CTAs are identical. The headline is what changes — and the direction is consistent: the rejected one promises the outcome, the approved one offers a chance at it.

The destination explains the split

Meta’s policy covers landing pages. Every Group B rejection points at the iOS App Store; every running twin points at Google Play. Those two listings are not the same text — and they differ on exactly the sentence that decides Meta’s money-game test.

Rejection rates by ad set are consistent with this: 9 of 26 on the iOS set, 4 of 26 on Android registration, 1 of 11 on Android install.

Why that delta matters

Meta’s test, quoted in your notice, is monetary value as a method of entry and monetary value as the prize. A destination check on the App Store page sees contests marked frequent, rewards “on the line”, in-app purchases enabled, a 16-and-over age gate and a responsible-play disclaimer — the full signature of real-money gaming — with the one line that rebuts the entry half missing. The Play page carries that rebuttal under a heading.

This is correlation, not proof a reviewer opened the page. But it matches the platform split exactly, it is a difference the client controls, and it is cheap to fix and re-test.

What to avoid, re-tested

Each row is now checked against an approved ad carrying the same element. Four of my earlier recommendations do not survive that test and are marked cleared.

PatternAs it appearedVerdictEvidence
Headlines that promise the outcome Claim your win · Feel the real win · Claim the BGIS slot · Earn a BGIS slot · We see a BGIS slot in your future · Play for your BGIS slot Avoid The one pattern that survives the evidence. Within every concept, the rejected variant promises the result and the approved variant poses a question or offers a chance. Everything else on those creatives is identical.
A cash figure as the headline ₹20,00,000 IS ON THE LINE! Avoid C006 V2 put the money at display size and was rejected everywhere. C006 V1 kept the same ₹20L in a small badge and is running. Prominence, not presence.
Unverifiable participation counts 5000+ squads have already registered Probably remove Named by Meta in the PCP notice — but the identical Android ad is running, so this cannot be the whole story. Still worth removing: you would have to evidence the number on request.
A money figure in a badge 20,00,000 IN REWARDS · ₹20L PRIZE POOL · 20L TOTAL PRIZE POOL Cleared Not a trigger on its own. Running right now on approved ads in this account. I previously told you to strip these — that was wrong.
The shared primary text compete for a share of the ₹20 lakh prize pool Cleared Not a trigger. All 63 ads in the account carry it, including the 34 currently running. Rewriting it would change nothing.
Deadline urgency REGISTER NOW — CLOSES OCT 28 Cleared Not a trigger. Appears unchanged on approved C011 V3 and C012 V2.
Hinglish har roz · abhi download karo Cleared Not a trigger. The Hinglish and English versions of C001 behave identically.
Third-party marks BGIS · BGMI · the rendered BGIS stage logo Cleared Withdrawn entirely. Both store listings name the publisher as KRAFTON, Inc. — the company that owns BGMI and runs BGIS. Battlin is a Krafton app using Krafton’s own marks. There is no licensing exposure and I should not have raised it.

Next steps

Reordered from my earlier version. The appeal advice in particular has reversed — four of these ads now have a concrete, checkable argument behind them.

  1. Align the App Store listing with the Play Store listing

    Highest value

    The cheapest fix with the clearest rationale, and entirely within the client’s control. Add the Play Store’s “REWARDS WORTH PLAYING FOR — No entry fees.” section to the App Store description, and reconsider the “PLAY RESPONSIBLY … responsible play” closer, which is the standard disclaimer of the gambling sector and is doing the client no favours on a page Meta may be checking. Krafton controls both listings.

  2. Appeal the four platform-split ads

    This week

    120251098188670718, 120251098197790718, 120251050178960718, 120251050178940718. The argument is concrete and checkable: identical image_hash, identical primary text, approved on Android, rejected on iOS. This reverses my earlier advice not to appeal — that was based on believing content caused every rejection.

  3. Fix the five content-driven creatives, headline only

    This week

    C011 V1 and V2, C012 V1 and V3, C006 V2. Keep the art, the badges, the cash figure and the CTA. Rewrite only the headline to offer a chance rather than promise a result, using the approved sibling in each concept as the template — it already cleared review with everything else unchanged.

  4. Re-submit iOS only after the listing is updated

    Sequenced

    If the destination reading is right, re-submitting the same iOS ads against an unchanged App Store page will fail again. Change the listing first, let it propagate, then re-submit one ad and watch the outcome before scaling.

  5. Do not rewrite the shared primary text

    Dropped

    It is on all 63 ads and 34 are running. Changing it costs creative time and fixes nothing. I previously called this the single highest-value fix; the control group shows it is not.

  6. Drop the Krafton IP concern

    Dropped

    Withdrawn. Both listings credit KRAFTON, Inc. as publisher — the owner of BGMI and organiser of BGIS. The client is using its own marks. There is nothing to clear.

Method. Comparisons use Meta’s own image_hash, so “identical creative’’ means the same stored image, not a visual judgement. Primary text was compared as exact strings. Platform is taken from each ad’s destination link — App Store or Play Store.

Limits. Meta never says which element it objected to, so the Group A headline pattern is inference from a consistent comparison, not a stated reason. The Group B destination finding is likewise correlational — the listings differ in the way the policy cares about and the split matches exactly, but nothing proves a reviewer opened either page. Both are testable: change one variable, re-submit one ad, watch the result.

Store listings read 26 Oct 2026 from the two URLs supplied, in the India storefront. Listings change; re-check before acting on the comparison.
